newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian buyers on sidelines ahead of USDA reports.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian buyers on sidelines ahead of USDA reports.

text.p: Regional grains and oilseeds buyers are the sidelines, waiting wait for the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report due later this week before deciding whether to enter the market, traders said on Thursday.

Aside from the recent purchases by Thailand and Malaysia of 100,000 tonnes of corn from Argentina for April shipment, most Southeast Asian buyers were sitting tight until they saw the numbers from the USDA, the traders said.
"It's just incredibly quiet all around the region. Everybody here is just waiting for the USDA figures to drop before doing anything," a U.S. trader said.
"The buyers will not be buying so much forward because they got burned last year," said a trader for a U.S. commodity house.

He was refering to the buying spree of many regional outfits in mid-1996 when they bought corn at around US$170 a tonne C&F believing that prices had reached their bottom, only to find grains futures prices diving further.

U.S. corn coming into Southeast Asia was quoted at around $138-$142 a tonne C&F for April/May delivery on board a Panamax vessel against $149-$150 a tonne C&F for February/April shipment late last year, traders said.

Argentine-origin corn is even cheaper. It was quoted by traders here at around $130-$135 a tonne C&F for May delivery. The Thais bought their corn for around $130 a tonne C&F while the Malaysians bought theirs for around $135-$136 a tonne C&F.

The March contract of the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) closed one U.S. cent up at $2.59-1/4 a bushel on Wednesday. The May contract was steady at $2.59-1/2 a bushel as people squared their positions ahead of the USDA reports.
Corn futures prices were hovering at around $2.65-$2.70 a bushel last month.
"The prices are already very attractive for buyers, but they'd rather wait for the USDA numbers first. Anyway, it's only one or two more days so what's the rush?" another dealer said.

"Malaysia has enough spot corn and they have more coming in. The Indonesians don't need any because their harvest will peak in the next few weeks. The Thais are out. Everyone has got more than enough corn. That side of the business is dead," a trader said.
Recent rumours about possible Chinese corn exports of up to two million tonnes were dismissed by dealers.
"The prices the Chinese were quoting for their corn are too high. You also have Argentinian stuff coming into the market and pushing prices lower," one trader said.
The only regional action traders see on the horizon would be spot demand for soymeal from some countries who may want to cover some of their open positions.

Traders said the Indonesians may be looking for a Panamax-sized shipment of soymeal for March-May delivery while Malaysian buyers will be looking for a Handy-sized shipment of soymeal for February-March delivery.
A Panamax can load about 50,000 tonnes of meal while a Handy would have up to 25,000 tonnes.

"The Indonesians will be looking for March onward while the Malaysians would want one Handy of meal. But they're both not in a hurry to buy. They have time to wait," a senior dealer for a European commodity trading company said.
"You have to understand, though, that it may or may not happen since buyers from both nations are not really pressed to buy the meal at the moment," another dealer said.

The price of U.S. soymeal coming into the region was quoted by dealers at about $275-$280 a tonne C&F for March/May shipment on board a Panamax against a quote late last month of around $294-$295 a tonne C&F for February/April devliery.

Indian-origin soymeal, on the other hand, was seen at around $295-$297 a tonne C&F for February/March shipment on a Tweendecker compared to a quote last month of $303-$307 a tonne C&F for January-February delivery, traders said.
"Most of the buying will be focused in northern Asia. The buyers here are fairly well-covered for now," one dealer said.

-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
